Guest Announcement: Nanoscience Student Society (NSS)

Before we dive into the physics today, we have a couple of special visitors from the Nanoscience Student Society (NSS). These are senior students in the nanomedicine track, and they are here to tell you why you should be very excited about getting involved!

NSS is a fantastic organization that combines graduate and professional development, mentorship, networking, and industry exposure. It is a great place to learn what nanoscience is all about, talk to upperclassmen to figure out your major, and get a head start on finding research opportunities.

They are currently working with the Nanoscale Characterization and Fabrication Laboratory (NCFL). If you aren’t familiar, the NCFL is our premier research center packed with different types of advanced microscopes and instrumentation. NSS is organizing a lab tour there soon, which is an incredible opportunity to see the equipment up close.

They hold bi-weekly meetings on Wednesdays at 6:00 PM. It is a great way to hang out outside of class, and yes—there is free food! I will include their contact information and upcoming event schedule below so you can scan the QR codes and get connected.

Recap: The Wave-Particle Duality of Electrons

Alright, where did we leave off last time? We were discussing the idea of using beams of electrons—or even individual electrons—to image things. Even though we tend to think of electrons as individual particles, like tiny ping-pong balls or BBs, they actually behave like waves.

Really, anything in the universe at the most fundamental level can behave like a particle or a wave. We often focus on electrons because they have practical, everyday uses in both forms.

So, how do we get a wavelength out of an electron? As long as the electron is moving, it has a quantity called momentum. We use a simple equation to find what is called the de Broglie wavelength. (It looks like "de Broglie," but it is pronounced "de Broy"—we determined last time that Dr. de Broglie might have been a "bro").

Here is the equation: \begin{align*} \lambda &= \frac{h}{p} \\ \lambda &= \frac{h}{m v} \end{align*}

In this formula, \lambda is the wavelength. We take Planck’s constant, h, which is a universal constant you can look up in any textbook, and divide it by the momentum, p. Momentum is simply the mass of the electron, m, multiplied by its velocity, v.

We found that electrons with high enough kinetic energy—meaning they are moving fast enough—have sufficiently short de Broglie wavelengths that we can use these electron waves to image really tiny things, even individual atoms!

Why Don’t Baseballs Behave Like Waves?

We ended our last class by asking ourselves a logical question: if an electron can behave like a wave, and physicists tell us that other subatomic particles like neutrons and protons can behave like waves, why don’t we? Why doesn’t a fast-traveling baseball, which has quite a bit of momentum, behave like a wave?

Look at Jacob Misiorowski throwing over 100 miles per hour. I don’t really see the baseball waving! I think the only thing waving is the batter’s bat as he misses the pitch. Let’s crunch some numbers to understand exactly why we don’t see the baseball acting like a wave.

Crunching the Numbers: The de Broglie Wavelength of a Fastball

What is the de Broglie wavelength of a baseball moving at 100 miles per hour? Let’s set up our variables.

The mass of a standard baseball, m, is about 0.15 \text{ kg}. The velocity, v, is 100 \text{ mph}. Planck’s constant, h, is roughly 6.6 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J}\cdot\text{s}.

You probably know what I am going to do with these numbers. I mean, who wants to deal with 6.6 and 0.15? We are going to round these into friendly powers of ten to make the mental math easy.

Let’s round Planck’s constant up to 10 \times 10^{-34}, which simplifies to 10^{-33}. A Joule is the standard unit for energy, made up of kilograms, meters, and seconds (\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2). So, we can write Planck’s constant as: \begin{align*} h &\approx 10^{-33} \frac{\text{kg} \cdot \text{m}^2}{\text{s}} \end{align*}

For the mass of the baseball, let’s round 0.15 \text{ kg} down to 0.1 \text{ kg}, which we can write in scientific notation as 10^{-1} \text{ kg}: \begin{align*} m &\approx 10^{-1} \text{ kg} \end{align*}

Now for the velocity. We have 100 \text{ mph}, but we need standard units of meters and seconds. Let’s do a quick unit conversion. I happen to know a mile is about 1600 \text{ meters} because, back when I was young and energetic, I ran mile races. I was not fast, so I never went below five minutes—it was very pathetic! And we know an hour has 3600 \text{ seconds}. \begin{align*} v &= 100 \frac{\text{miles}}{\text{hr}} \times \left( \frac{1600 \text{ m}}{1 \text{ mile}} \right) \times \left( \frac{1 \text{ hr}}{3600 \text{ s}} \right) \end{align*}

Again, who wants to deal with 1600 and 3600? Let’s round 1600 down to 1000 (10^3). For 3600, it is kind of on the borderline. Fun fact: in a log scale, 3000 is exactly halfway between 1000 and 10,000. That might show up on a quiz, maybe not! We’ll see. Anyway, let’s just round 3600 down to 1000 (10^3) as well. \begin{align*} v &\approx 10^2 \times \left( \frac{10^3 \text{ m}}{10^3 \text{ s}} \right) \\ v &\approx 10^2 \text{ m/s} \end{align*}

So, 100 \text{ mph} is roughly 100 \text{ m/s}. If you think about a 100-meter sprint or the length of a football field, a fastball covers that distance in about one second. That makes intuitive sense!

Now, let’s plug all these friendly numbers back into our de Broglie equation: \begin{align*} \lambda &\approx \frac{10^{-33} \frac{\text{kg} \cdot \text{m}^2}{\text{s}}}{(10^{-1} \text{ kg}) \times (10^2 \text{ m/s})} \\ \lambda &\approx \frac{10^{-33}}{10^1} \text{ m} \\ \lambda &\approx 10^{-34} \text{ m} \end{align*}

We end up with an incredibly small length: 10^{-34} meters. I want to remind you all just how ridiculously small this is. The size of an atom is about 10^{-10} meters (one divided by ten billion). This baseball’s wavelength is one divided by a number with 34 trailing zeros! Just for your entertainment, here is what that fraction looks like: \begin{align*} \lambda &\approx \frac{1}{10,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000} \text{ m} \end{align*}

Is there really anything in the universe this small? For practical purposes, no. The atom is usually the smallest entity we deal with. If you are into theoretical physics, there is a length scale called the Planck length. Some physicists suggest that if the universe is like a computer screen, the Planck length is the minimum "pixel size" of space. Our baseball’s wavelength is right around that scale!

The point is that the de Broglie wavelength of a 100 mph baseball is so small that you would never see it behave like a wave. You would never see it diffract, because you simply cannot make a slit or aperture small enough for it to squeeze through.

The crazy thing about quantum mechanics is that there is always a non-zero probability that anything can happen. There is even a non-zero chance that I could walk straight through the classroom wall! But I would have to try it many, many times, and it would probably take several times longer than the age of the universe to actually happen. So, in real life, a baseball is just a particle.

The Double-Slit Experiment: A Quantum Mystery

With electrons, however, if you are in the right speed range, the wavelength is large enough that you can actually see them diffract when passed through small slits. This brings us to a famous, mind-bending experiment.

If you shoot classical particles—like bullets from a gun—through two narrow slits, you expect them to form two distinct bands on the backstop. If you send waves—like water ripples—through two slits, the waves diffract and interfere with each other, creating a stripy interference pattern of constructive and destructive waves.

So, what happens if we build an electron gun and fire electrons one at a time at two slits?

Since we are firing them individually, you might expect them to act like bullets and form two bands. But remember, electrons can behave like waves!

I won’t spoil the final outcome for you here in the notes. I am going to upload an extra credit assignment where you will hypothesize what happens, watch the video of the actual experiment, and summarize your observations.

As you will see when you watch the video, there is no straightforward, intuitive classical analogue for this behavior. It is fundamentally weird—we have something behaving as both a wave and a particle, a "wavicle."

Why Does This "Weirdness" Matter?

Even though this wave-particle duality is nonclassical and relies on probabilistic behavior, it is incredibly useful! Let’s look at a couple of areas where this weird behavior is essential to modern technology and chemistry.

Quantum Computing and Qubits

In classical computing, information is stored in bits. A classical bit is always either a 0 or a 1. Think of it like a light switch that is either strictly off or strictly on.

In quantum computing, we use quantum bits, or "qubits." Because of quantum mechanics, a qubit can exist in a "superposition" of 0 and 1 at the same time. We can write this superposition mathematically using a special notation that physicists love: \begin{align*} |\psi\rangle &= \alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle \end{align*}

In this equation, |\psi\rangle is just a fancy way to write the state of our quantum system. The terms |0\rangle and |1\rangle represent the classical states of 0 and 1. The symbols \alpha and \beta are coefficients that tell us the probability of the qubit being measured as a 0 or a 1.

Accuracy Note

Possible error: This misstates the physical meaning of the amplitudes. The probabilities of measuring 0 or 1 are given by |\alpha|^2 and |\beta|^2, not by \alpha and \beta themselves.

Correction: \alpha and \beta are complex probability amplitudes; the actual measurement probabilities are |\alpha|^2 and |\beta|^2, which must sum to 1.

This is kind of like how an electron can go through two slits at the same time! This superposition allows quantum computers to perform many combinations of calculations simultaneously, making them incredibly powerful for solving complex problems that would take classical computers thousands of years.

Atomic Orbitals and Probability Maps

Wave-particle duality also explains how atoms are structured. You might have seen older diagrams where electrons orbit the nucleus in neat little circles, like planets orbiting the sun. But because electrons behave like waves, they aren’t simply "orbiting" in a fixed path.

Instead, they exist in "atomic orbitals," which are essentially 3D probability maps. These maps tell us the likelihood of finding an electron in a specific region around the nucleus. These orbitals—like the s, p, d, and f orbitals you might remember from high school chemistry—are derived by solving Schrödinger’s wave equation. The electron is spread out like a wave, and its exact position remains probabilistic until we interact with it.
